adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code increments `match_count` and sets `last_match_at` then calls `record.save` without checking success or handling failure. While this likely won’t fail due to the shown validations (email isn’t changed and is present), a failed save (e.g., unexpected validation/DB issue) would silently drop the stats update and the caller wouldn’t know.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:14 — Blocked emails produce a distinct message (`user.email.blocked` "is not allowed.") vs `not_allowed`/uniqueness, and `errors.to_hash` is returned verbatim from users#create, letting an unauthenticated attacker enumerate the blocked list and pump `match_count` with repeated POSTs.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a distinct validation error for blocked emails (`EmailValidator` adds `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')` when `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is true) while other email failures use different messages (`user.email.not_allowed`, uniqueness/presence). In `UsersController#create`, failures now render `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`, exposing the specific email error to the client. Together, this allows a client to distinguish “blocked” vs other invalid emails by observing the returned `errors`/message. Additionally, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count` and updates `last_match_at` on every match (regardless of action_type), so repeated POSTs using a known blocked email will pump those counters.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — record.errors[attribute].blank?` short-circuit means a blocked email that also fails presence/uniqueness/whitelist/blacklist never reaches `should_block?`, so `match_count`/`last_match_at` are never recorded for those attempts and the "have we ever seen this email" stat the spec relies on is unreliable.

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, the blocked-email check is guarded by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. Since other validations (whitelist/blacklist in this same validator, and potentially presence/uniqueness from other validators on `:email`) can populate `record.errors[:email]` first, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` won’t be called in those cases—so `match_count`/`last_match_at` won’t be updated for those attempts. This doesn’t break rejection behavior (the user is already invalid), but it does make the blocked-email statistics incomplete.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — Any email error (including "has already been taken" or domain not allowed) pushes the email into `rejectedEmails`, after which the client permanently reports it as `user.email.invalid`, hiding the real reason and blocking resubmission for the whole session even if the server-side condition changes.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed signup response with `result.errors.email` causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (lines ~271-275). The email validation logic then short-circuits on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and always returns a failure with `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (lines ~65-73), masking the actual server-side reason (e.g. `user.email.not_allowed`, `user.email.blocked`, or uniqueness) and making that email permanently fail client-side validation for the rest of the session (due to the `rejectedEmails.@each` dependency).

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/user.rb:47 — validates :email, email: true` resolves `EmailValidator` at class-load time; the diff adds lib/validators/email_validator.rb but includes no autoload_path change for lib/validators, so User itself fails to load (ArgumentError: Unknown validator) unless that path is already autoloaded.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `User` to use a custom validator (`validates :email, email: true`) but adds the validator at `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` with a top-level `EmailValidator` constant. The diff contains no change to autoload/eager_load paths to include `lib/validators`, and in typical Rails autoloading the constant `EmailValidator` maps to `email_validator.rb` (not `validators/email_validator.rb`). Without additional configuration elsewhere, this can raise `ArgumentError: Unknown validator: 'EmailValidator'` when loading `User`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:8 — Enum` is referenced but not defined anywhere in this change (no lib/enum.rb present), so `BlockedEmail.actions` / `set_defaults` raise NameError on first use unless Enum already exists in the codebase.

From the diff alone, `Enum` is an external dependency that must already exist elsewhere in the codebase; if it doesn’t, this would raise `NameError`. The finding correctly notes the dependency is not introduced in this change, but whether it is actually undefined cannot be verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:201 — If the blocked_emails migration has not run, `should_block?` raises `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` which users#create rescues and reports as "something already taken", masking the missing table and turning every signup into a misleading failure.

The exact claim about the rescue being reported specifically as “something already taken” isn’t verifiable from the diff snippet, but the masking behavior is diff-grounded and newly more likely due to the added table dependency.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:269 — The change_email flow only checks uniqueness manually and never runs EmailValidator, so an existing user can switch to a blocked or blacklisted address; the block check is enforced only via `if: :email_changed?` on User.save which this path does not use.

adjudication.rationale: The provided diff only changes `UsersController#create` to include `errors` and `values` in the JSON response; it does not show any `change_email` flow or a path that “only checks uniqueness manually” and bypasses `User.save` validations. Since the alleged issue refers to code at `users_controller.rb:269` and behavior not present or modified in this diff, it can’t be verified from the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count += 1; save` is a read-modify-write with no lock or `increment_counter`, so concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose updates.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save`. This is a classic read-modify-write sequence without any locking or atomic increment. If two signups hit the same blocked email concurrently, both can read the same `match_count` and write back the same incremented value, losing one update (and potentially overwriting `last_match_at`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined on the class prototype, so the array is shared across all instances and never reset when the modal is reopened.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` as a mutable array property on the controller definition (`Discourse.Controller.extend(...)`). In Ember, such prototype-level mutable objects are shared and persist unless explicitly reinitialized per instance/open. The diff shows `rejectedEmails` being appended to (`pushObject(result.values.email)`) and used to hard-fail validation (`contains(email)`), but there is no corresponding reset/clear anywhere in the shown changes. This means rejected emails can persist beyond the intended lifecycle (e.g., reopening the modal) and can incorrectly block future submissions without re-checking the server.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — rejectedEmails.contains(email)` is a case-sensitive exact compare against the server-returned value, so retyping the same address with different case bypasses the client-side rejection (server also does no normalization, see P1).

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the new `rejectedEmails` cache uses `contains(email)` (strict string equality), so `Test@Example.com` vs `test@example.com` will not match and the client-side short-circuit won’t trigger. The server-side blocked check is also case-sensitive: `EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` does an exact match with no normalization/downcasing shown in the diff. This allows bypassing blocked emails by changing case, which is a real correctness/security gap in the newly added blocked email functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:72 — Client discards the server-provided `errors.email` message (e.g. new `user.email.blocked`) and shows the generic `user.email.invalid` text instead, so the new `errors` payload is only used as a boolean.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — values.email` is the raw un-normalized value (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] directly), so `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` is a case-sensitive exact match and re-typing the address with different case bypasses the client-side guard (server re-validates, so no security impact).

Ember array `contains` performs an exact match, so the guard is inherently case-sensitive and can be bypassed by retyping the same address with different casing. The claim that the server value is definitely “raw/un-normalized” cannot be verified from this diff, but the case-sensitive bypass of the new guard is diff-grounded; server-side validation still runs so it’s not a security/correctness defect in final enforcement.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact case-sensitive `where(email:)` lookup while User never downcases email, so "Block@Spam.org" bypasses a "block@spam.org" entry (the removed domain check was case-insensitive).

adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same underlying bypass risk: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive exact email lookup, so an email with different casing (e.g., User@Example.com / Block@Spam.org) can evade an existing blocked entry stored in lowercase, potentially allowing access that should be blocked.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — should_block? mutates/saves the record inside validation, and users#create calls `user.valid?` then `user.save`, so match_count/last_match_at are bumped twice per signup attempt and on every unrelated `valid?` call.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) when there are no prior email errors. BlockedEmail.should_block? (app/models/blocked_email.rb:12-19) mutates persistent state (increments match_count/updates last_match_at and saves) during validation. Since Rails validations can run multiple times in a request (e.g., User#save triggers validations, and any explicit #valid? elsewhere would also trigger them), a single signup attempt can bump these counters multiple times, and any other validations on a User with a blocked email will also update BlockedEmail stats as a side effect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write (`+= 1; save`) so concurrent signups lose counts; use `increment!`/`update_all`.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code loads a record and then does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a non-atomic read-modify-write sequence, so concurrent signups hitting the same blocked email can overwrite each other’s increments and lose counts. The diff shows this exact pattern at `app/models/blocked_email.rb` lines updating `match_count`/`last_match_at`, and an atomic update method (`increment!`, `update_columns`, or `update_all` with SQL increment) would avoid the race.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard skips the BlockedEmail check whenever presence/uniqueness/domain already failed, so blocked-email stats are not recorded for those attempts and the error message differs by ordering.

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, the blocked-email check is gated by `record.errors[attribute].blank?` (line with `and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), so `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (which increments `match_count`/`last_match_at`) will not run if earlier validations (whitelist/blacklist in this validator, or presence/uniqueness validations declared before it in `user.rb`) have already populated `errors[:email]`. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral consequence (stats not updated; error message determined by earlier failure), but whether it’s a “defect” vs intended ordering is not provable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — Any `errors.email` (e.g. "already taken" uniqueness error) pushes the email into rejectedEmails, after which the field permanently shows the generic `user.email.invalid` reason for that address.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails` and makes `emailValidation` immediately fail with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` whenever `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` (create_account_controller.js). On account creation failure, it pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` is present, regardless of which email error it was (e.g., uniqueness/already taken, domain not allowed, blocked). Since nothing ever removes that email from `rejectedEmails`, that specific address will thereafter always show the generic "invalid" reason client-side and block/override more specific messaging for that same email.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined on the prototype and never reset, so rejections persist for the page lifetime across modal open/close and controller instances.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined as a mutable array literal on the object prototype (`Discourse.Controller.extend(...)`). In Ember this means the same array instance can be shared and will persist unless explicitly reset. The diff shows `pushObject(result.values.email)` on failed signup, but no code that clears `rejectedEmails` on modal close/reset, so once an email is added it will continue to trigger the early `contains(email)` failure path on subsequent uses within the same page lifetime (and potentially across instances if more than one controller instance is ever created).

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — action_type is NOT NULL with no DB default; the only default lives in BlockedEmail#set_defaults (before_validation), so the manual/CSV table loads the spec explicitly anticipates ("If we manually load the table") will fail with a not-null violation unless action_type is supplied.

That means inserts that bypass Rails validations/callbacks (e.g., manual SQL/CSV imports) will hit a NOT NULL violation unless `action_type` is provided. This is a real, diff-grounded operational/schema concern, not an in-app runtime defect for normal Rails-created records.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:10 — Unique index is case-sensitive and BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact `where(email:)` match while User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] verbatim (no downcase), so "Bad@Spam.com" bypasses a "bad@spam.com" row and both casings can coexist; add a unique index on lower(email) and normalise on lookup/insert.

From the diff, this means different email casings (e.g. `Bad@Spam.com` vs `bad@spam.com`) can evade a block row and/or be inserted as distinct records, depending on DB collation; in Postgres (typical for Discourse), this is a real bypass/duplication issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — BlockedEmail.should_block? is invoked from inside User validation, so every User#valid?/save with a changed email now performs a SELECT on blocked_emails plus, on a match, a full BlockedEmail#save (its own uniqueness SELECT + UPDATE) as a side effect of validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168 — users#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, so the EmailValidator (and should_block?'s SELECT/UPDATE side effects) runs twice per signup, double-counting match_count and doubling the blocked_emails round-trips.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count is incremented via read-modify-write and a full save rather than an atomic UPDATE (update_all "match_count = match_count + 1" / update_counters), causing lost updates and row-lock contention on hot blocked emails under concurrent signups.

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb#should_block?, the code does `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` then `record.match_count += 1` and `record.save`. This is a non-atomic read-modify-write sequence, so concurrent signups hitting the same blocked email can overwrite each other’s increments (lost updates) and add extra row-lock/save overhead. An atomic update (e.g., update_counters/update_all) would avoid the race.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — record.save runs BlockedEmail validations (including the uniqueness SELECT on email) on every match even though email is unchanged; use save(validate: false) or an atomic counter update to avoid the extra query.

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb#should_block?, when a matching record exists it increments match_count, sets last_match_at, then calls record.save. Because BlockedEmail has `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true`, this `save` will run validations each time (including a uniqueness lookup on `email`) even though `email` isn’t changing, adding unnecessary DB work on every match. This is a concrete, diff-grounded performance/implementation concern rather than a correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — Statistics are written (UPDATE) even for action_type :do_nothing records, so every match of a no-op entry still incurs the write; consider only recording stats for :block or batching counters.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and calls `record.save` for any matching record before checking `record.action_type == actions[:block]`. This means `:do_nothing` entries still incur a DB write on every match. That’s a real, diff-grounded performance/architecture concern, but not a correctness defect since tracking stats for no-op entries could be intentional.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:21 — Regexp.new is rebuilt from the SiteSetting string on every validation (and twice per signup); cache the compiled regexp keyed on the setting value.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `email_in_restriction_setting?` builds a new `Regexp` each time it is called (`regexp = Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`). Since `validate_each` calls this helper whenever `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` or `..._blacklist` is present, the regexp will be recompiled on every validation invocation for those settings. This is a concrete performance concern introduced/embodied by the new validator, but it does not constitute a correctness bug based on the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:21 — Domain regex `@(domains)` is unanchored and case-insensitive, so a whitelist of `gmail.com` is bypassed by `user@gmail.com.attacker.net` or `user@gmail.company` and the blacklist is evaded by `user@evil.com@gmail.com`-style values because no `$`/`\z` anchor or email-format check exists.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point to the same core flaw: the domain-matching regex `@(domains)` is not properly anchored/boundaried to the end of the email domain, so whitelisted domains like `example.com` can be bypassed with subdomains/suffixes such as `evil.example.com` or `gmail.com.attacker.net`. The candidate’s examples and mention of missing `$`/`\z` anchoring align with the golden issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — BlockedEmail.should_block?` does an exact, case-sensitive `where(email: email)` on the raw signup value with no downcase/strip normalization (User has none either), so `Blocked@Spam.org` or ` blocked@spam.org` trivially bypasses a block on `blocked@spam.org`.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` (app/models/blocked_email.rb) the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact match on the raw input value. The new `EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` without any normalization, and the diff shows no downcasing/stripping of `User#email` before validation or persistence. As a result, a block entry for `blocked@spam.org` can be bypassed by signing up with a case/whitespace-variant like `Blocked@Spam.org` or ` blocked@spam.org`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — Blocked-list check is only run after whitelist/blacklist pass and returns a distinct "is not allowed." message (vs. the domain message), letting an unauthenticated caller of users#create probe whether any specific address is on the BlockedEmail table.

This enables probing membership in the `blocked_emails` table, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — should_block?` performs a DB write (match_count/last_match_at save) inside model validation reachable from the unauthenticated, CSRF-exempt users#create endpoint, allowing anyone to pollute block statistics or generate unbounded writes per request.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a side-effecting validation: `User` now runs `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, and `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a DB write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) whenever a matching `blocked_emails` row exists. Since `users_controller#create` triggers user validations during account creation, an unauthenticated client can repeatedly submit a blocked email to cause unbounded writes and pollute the block statistics. (The CSRF-exempt detail isn’t shown in the diff, but the write-on-validation behavior and reachability from `create` are.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — New `errors: user.errors.to_hash` exposes a machine-readable per-field `email: ["has already been taken"]` to unauthenticated callers, making account/email enumeration easier (the text was already in `message`, so this is a hardening regression rather than a new leak).

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the failure JSON now includes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. Since this endpoint is used for account creation (typically unauthenticated), returning structured per-field validation errors (e.g., `email: ["has already been taken"]`) makes automated account/email enumeration easier than the previous single combined `message` string, constituting a security hardening regression introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — Only `.` is escaped before interpolating the SiteSetting into `Regexp.new`; other metacharacters (`(`, `*`, `+`, `?`) from an admin-entered domain list are interpreted, enabling malformed/catastrophic patterns instead of using `Regexp.escape` per domain.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? builds a regex from the admin-provided SiteSetting by only escaping '.' (setting.gsub('.', '\\.')) and then interpolating it into Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true). Any other regex metacharacters in the setting (e.g., '(', '*', '+', '?', '|', '\\') will be interpreted as regex syntax, potentially causing malformed regexes or catastrophic backtracking. Using Regexp.escape (or escaping per-domain tokens) would avoid regex injection/perf issues.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:20 — No test for case-insensitive matching: should_block? uses an exact `where(email:)` (app/models/blocked_email.rb:12) so "Block@spamfromhome.org" would bypass the block and the uniqueness validation; neither behavior is pinned by a spec.

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does an exact match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`), and the model also uses a case-sensitive uniqueness validation (`validates :email, ... uniqueness: true`).
